So we will check if the file is binary, even if it means loading the whole thing in memory (but if you _have_ a streaming API, then obviously you should only load the first 4K to make that determination. And use the `-diff` gitattribute, of course. Git doesn't do the streaming thing now, but it should). The size of the file never impacts the decision on whether it's binary. But once we know it's binary, then we can avoid loading it if we haven't already.

column1: We do a similar thing with filters. We used to fail to run filters for the large-file streaming code paths, but that's wrong. You can't stream in the face of filters (well, you can, but it's tricky), so now we do the correct thing, and avoid the optimization if we have to.

In practice I doubt it comes up much, because large files _are_ going to be binary. So it's important to be optimistic about making sure the optimizations work in the common cases, but fail to slow-but-correct if we have to.

column1: Also, I suspect some backends may want to support the ""match"" behavior natively instead of relying on the wrapper to do all the regex matching for them. It would be nice to pass in the pattern (or NULL) as a parameter when the iterator is initialized. That way, the backend can choose to narrow the search. (E.g. if your config backend is a database, it could do a select narrowed by the pattern so that the traversal of the matching config items was very efficient.)

I'm on the fence about whether we need a way for the backend to communicate if it supports the pattern matching, or if the front end should just always apply the pattern filtering knowing that with a smart backend, the patterns will just match 100% of the time.
